transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Ava Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Samuel Lee (Willowbank CTO), Priya Nair (Head of MLOps), Ethan Zhou (SecOps), Maya Brooks (Product), Tom Hernandez (SRE)

Summary (auto):
Willowbank is evaluating Redwood Dedicated vs Hosted/Private for LLM inference. Primary drivers: data isolation, steady baseline throughput for customer-facing features, burst capacity for end-of-month batch jobs, and predictable unit economics. Security and auditability (SOC2, KMS, VPC) are gating items. Next steps: pricing, security docs, and SE-led benchmark.

Topics: dedicated capacity, reserved GPUs, isolation needs, burst strategy, autoscaling, SLOs, security/compliance, benchmarking

Transcript:
[00:00] Ava Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'll kick us off. I'm Ava from Redwood, AE on the account, and with me is Diego, our solutions engineer.
[00:12] Samuel Lee: Hi, Samuel here. Thanks, appreciate you taking the time.
[00:15] Priya Nair: Priya from MLOps, curious about the dedicated offering details.
[00:20] Diego Morales: Great, quick agenda - we'll do a short discovery of your current stack and traffic, review Redwood Dedicated capabilities and isolation, and then surface options for autoscaling and burst. Save time at the end for questions.
[00:32] Tom Hernandez: Quick note from SRE - we'll want concrete metrics around latency and cost per token, and how burst works without violating our network isolation rules.
[00:40] Ava Chen: Perfect. Samuel, can you share the current use case and scale?
[00:45] Samuel Lee: Sure. We run a conversational assistant and a few summarization pipelines. Baseline is roughly 3 million tokens/day, peaking end of month to about 6-7M. Typical concurrency for low-latency API is ~300 QPS, with spikes to ~1.2k during promos. We need sub-200ms tail latency for short prompts.
[01:20] Diego Morales: Okay, that's helpful. Are you currently using hosted LLM providers or self-hosted?
[01:25] Priya Nair: We mix - experiments on OpenAI for proto, but for production we self-host an open model on k8s with our own A100s. Managing infra has been painful, which is why we're exploring Redwood.
[01:40] Maya Brooks: Cost and predictability are big for product - we want stable monthly spend and a path to handle bursts without overprovisioning.
[01:50] Ava Chen: That maps to Dedicated - reserved GPU pools give predictable throughput and isolated tenancy. You can configure a baseline commit and then set up burst capacity for short periods. For private/hybrid needs, Redwood Private provides customer-managed VPC options.
[02:10] Ethan Zhou: On the security side we have to validate KMS, SAML, RBAC, and audit logging. Also need SOC2 and encryption at rest. How does Redwood handle keys and logs?
[02:25] Diego Morales: We integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key management in Private or Dedicated with VPC peering. Audit logs are exported to your logging endpoint (s3, splunk, or our audit stream). SOC2 report available - we'll share that.
[02:40] Samuel Lee: For dedicated - is the control plane still managed? We require network isolation but don't want to manage the runtime.
[02:50] Ava Chen: Right - with Dedicated you get isolated GPU pools and tenant isolation while Redwood manages the runtime; for full air-gap you can go Private with a customer-controlled control plane.
[03:05] Tom Hernandez: Can you explain burst capacity? If we commit to 10 GPUs baseline, can we suddenly spin up another 20 for a few hours? How is billing handled?
[03:20] Diego Morales: Good question. Burst is configurable - you pick a burst bucket or pay-as-you-go burst. Typical pattern: baseline reserved capacity (monthly commit) for cost predictability, plus a burst buffer for short-term overages billed at a premium rate. We'll show examples in the pricing doc.
[03:40] Priya Nair: Latency is sensitive - our SLO is 200ms P95 for short responses. How does Redwood ensure latency with batching and KV cache?
[03:52] Diego Morales: The runtime supports continuous batching and prefix/KV caching, and we do kernel selection optimized for model and hardware. For low-latency endpoints we can pin capacity and tune batching windows to keep P95 low. There's a tradeoff: aggressive batching reduces cost but can increase latency, so you configure per-route.
[04:18] Samuel Lee: What GPUs do you run? We're interested in H100 vs A100, and mixed fleets.
[04:25] Ava Chen: We support both - Dedicated pools can be provisioned with H100 for high throughput/low latency, or A100 for cost-optimized runs. We also allow mixed clusters and routing policies to send high-priority low-latency traffic to H100 nodes.
[04:45] Maya Brooks: For compliance, we need data residency in our region and cannot have data leave the VPC. Is that possible with Dedicated?
[04:55] Diego Morales: Yes - Dedicated in a specific region, with private networking and optional VPC peering keeps traffic in-region. For strict residency we recommend Private deployment where you control the VPC.
[05:12] Ethan Zhou: On encryption, does Redwood manage keys or do we keep them in our KMS?
[05:18] Diego Morales: You can bring-your-own-keys (BYOK) and we can integrate with AWS KMS, GCP KMS, or an HSM. For full Private we can support on-prem HSMs.
[05:30] Samuel Lee: Let's talk scale: our forecast is doubling in 6 months, and a steady growth. How does scaling work operationally?
[05:40] Ava Chen: Autoscaling policies can be time-based and load-based. For Dedicated you can autoscale within the pool but to keep cost predictability most customers keep a reserved baseline and allow autoscale for buffer. For big capacity increases we coordinate additional reserved capacity with advance notice.
[06:00] Tom Hernandez: What level of isolation? Are there noisy neighbor issues if two customers are on same hardware?
[06:08] Diego Morales: Dedicated is tenant-isolated by pool - no other tenants share the same GPUs. For additional isolation you can choose physical isolation racks or Private deployment.
[06:18] Priya Nair: Any preflight or onboarding steps? We have internal change windows and security reviews.
[06:25] Ava Chen: We do an onboarding checklist: onboard security docs, network setup, test workloads, and then a pilot phase. Typical pilot is 2-4 weeks with agreed benchmarks.
[06:38] Samuel Lee: About benchmarks - we'd like a SE-led run using our sample prompts and traffic. What artifacts do you need?
[06:45] Diego Morales: Ideally: sample prompt set, typical seq lengths, concurrency profile, and any special model variants or quantization preferences. We'll also need keys to your test endpoints if you want to run comparative tests.
[06:58] Priya Nair: We use INT8 quantization on our self-hosted models right now - will Redwood support that?
[07:05] Diego Morales: Yes, the runtime supports quantized models and we have quantization-friendly exec paths. We'll surface performance deltas and recommend profiles per workload.
[07:18] Maya Brooks: How are rollouts handled - can we do canary traffic or A/B?
[07:25] Ava Chen: Yes - Redwood Console supports canary deploys, A/B routing, and automatic fallback to a lower-cost model if latencies spike.
[07:36] Samuel Lee: Costs - ballpark numbers for reserved capacity vs hosted?
[07:42] Ava Chen: We'll share a pricing sheet. High level: reserved commitments reduce unit cost substantially compared to on-demand; dedicated baseline is priced monthly by GPU-equivalent capacity plus network. Burst is billed separately. We'll send concrete examples for your traffic profile.
[07:58] Tom Hernandez: On monitoring - we need token-level lineage, per-route latency breakdowns, and tracing hooks to our existing APM.
[08:08] Diego Morales: Redwood Console provides per-route/model dashboards, token cost breakdowns, and tracing integrations (Jaeger/OTel). Logs and metrics can be forwarded to your observability stack.
[08:22] Samuel Lee: Any gotchas around model compatibility? We're using a trimmed down LlamaX fork.
[08:30] Diego Morales: We onboard custom models; sometimes ops configuration or tokenizer differences cause hiccups. Our model onboarding team handles eversioning; we surface any incompatibilities up front.
[08:42] Priya Nair: How long to provision Dedicated baseline?
[08:46] Ava Chen: Typically 2-4 weeks for standard suites; if you need physical racks or on-prem it'll be longer.
[08:54] Ethan Zhou: Regarding audit - we need immutable audit logs and ability to demonstrate data deletion policies.
[09:00] Diego Morales: We retain audit logs per your retention policy and can provide exports for audits. We also support customer-driven retention and deletion lifecycle controls.
[09:12] Maya Brooks: For burst routing, can we prioritize certain tenants or routes?
[09:18] Diego Morales: Yes - routing policies allow priority lanes, rate limits, and fallback rules. You can send high-value traffic to reserved capacity and overflow to burst.
[09:30] Samuel Lee: Any reference customers in finance?
[09:34] Ava Chen: We have a few mid-market banks on Dedicated - we'll anonymize references and share case studies.
[09:40] Tom Hernandez: On SLAs - what uptime/latency SLAs are available for Dedicated?
[09:46] Diego Morales: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets; details vary by contract tier. We'll include SLA language in the follow-up.
[09:58] Priya Nair: For the SE benchmarking, can you simulate our peak spikes? We want to see behavior at 1.2k concurrency and end-of-month volumes.
[10:06] Diego Morales: Absolutely - if you give us the traffic profile and sample prompts we'll run comparative tests across H100/A100 and quantify cost/latency tradeoffs.
[10:18] Samuel Lee: Also need to validate data residency and that logs don't leave region.
[10:24] Ava Chen: We'll confirm region-specific deployment and network topology options.
[10:30] Ethan Zhou: A few quick security questions: SOC2 type II, penetration test cadence, and whether you provide a penetration test report?
[10:38] Diego Morales: We have SOC2 Type II and regular pentests. We can share a redacted pentest summary and SOC2 attestation under NDA.
[10:46] Maya Brooks: What's the contract term options? Monthly, annual? Any incentives for commit?
[10:52] Ava Chen: Standard is monthly or annual commits. Annual reserved commits typically get better unit pricing. We'll include sample T&Cs in the follow-up.
[10:59] Tom Hernandez: For integration - how intrusive is the networking setup? We prefer minimal changes to our VPC firewall rules.
[11:06] Diego Morales: For Dedicated with VPC peering it's a small set of CIDR exchanges and route rules. For Private there's more setup but we provide a network runbook.
[11:18] Samuel Lee: Ok, let's summarize next steps. Priya, we'll share traffic profiles; Ethan will compile security questions; Ava will send pricing and security docs; Diego will prepare a benchmark plan.
[11:32] Priya Nair: Sounds good. I'll push the SLO and traffic artifacts today/tomorrow.
[11:36] Ethan Zhou: I'll gather the KMS/HSM vendor info and our security checklist.
[11:40] Ava Chen: Great - we'll target the SE deep-dive next week. Diego, any final notes?
[11:45] Diego Morales: Nothing more. We'll prepare a proposed test matrix (H100 vs A100, quantized vs fp16), and include example request traces.
[11:54] Samuel Lee: Appreciate it - look forward to the docs.
[11:58] Ava Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the materials and a calendar invite for the benchmark deep-dive.
[12:03] (call ends)
